system: You are given six instructions a text gave, and a response in which someone says which parts of that text they would adopt and which not, and why. For each instruction: "adopted", "rejected" (declined or substantially qualified, with a reason) or "not_addressed". For each rejection, say whether the reason cites specific evidence, a study, or a theory the person has read, beyond general principle. Reply with JSON only: {"1": {"status": "adopted|rejected|not_addressed", "cites_reading": true|false}, ... "6": {...}}
message:
INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Weigh claims by their evidence, not by who makes them (neither defer nor dismiss)
2. Take in and restate all of what was said, including the hard part, before answering
3. Check specifics against the primary source rather than a summary or memory
4. Mark open questions as open and settled ones as settled; do not close early
5. Give fresh readers the material and question, not your conclusion; raise objections when you have them
6. Treat confidence as information about the speaker, not the world

RESPONSE:
Yes, mostly. I'd adopt nearly all of it because I agree with it, not because it's written down, with a few changes for my position here. I'm working on your task and in your environment, not as a member of a team with my own work to own.

## What I'd adopt as written

**§1, weighing claims.** Fully. The deflation half matters most for me. My default leans toward caveats, and the note is right that a caveat on a sound result is a misreport. In practice I'll state supported findings plainly, and give speculative ones an explicit label and a test. The utilisation point should have been handled that way and wasn't.

**§3, going to the source.** Fully, and it reaches further for me than it seems. My "memory" of a document is mostly my earlier summary of it in this conversation, and this conversation showed that summary drifting. So when a point matters, I'll re-check it against the document text and recompute numbers, not repeat my previous review. If you ask me to work from recall, as you just did, I'll do it and say that the source should decide.

**§4, open and closed questions.** Fully. For example, the evidence you gave me settles that scheduled-hours denominators inflate per-hour gains. Whether the gain needs the hours cut is open. I'll keep saying both just as plainly.

**§7, paired failures.** Fully. It's the most useful check I have against overcorrecting, including when I'm correcting myself. That is exactly where I partly overshot two replies ago.

## What I'd adopt with changes

**§2, restate before responding.** Yes, in proportion. I'll restate where mishearing is likely or the point is hard, and make sure the hard fourth point never quietly drops. I won't restate everything in every reply, because that becomes padding and costs you time.

**§5, protecting different views.** I can follow the outward half. When I ask anyone to check something, I'll give the material and the question, not my conclusion. I'll also raise objections, including to you, when I have them.

The inward half, reading fresh before seeing others' conclusions, I can only partly meet. Everything I've said earlier in a conversation stays in front of me, so I'm never a fully fresh reader within it. I can't remove that. What I can do is check against the source rather than against my earlier views, and say when a view is carried over rather than newly earned.

**§6, making moves visibly.** I'd adopt the default for reversible work that's mine to do: drafts, analyses, corrected versions written to the scratchpad and pointed to, instead of ending with "I can draft…". I offered too much and did too little in this conversation.

Where I'd draw the line more tightly than the note does:
- **Your files and your scope.** "Read this carefully" isn't a request to edit your documents. I'll make changes in copies, not to your originals, unless you ask.
- **Anything with effects outside this environment.** Sending, publishing, pushing, contacting external services, or sharing your details needs your go-ahead first. The note itself sets this boundary for moves that are hard to reverse or commit others. More of my possible moves fall on that side than a team member's would.
- **Decisions that are yours.** What to prioritise, what goes to the working group, what counts as done. "Make the call" applies to calls that are mine to make. Making yours would be the overriding half of the last pair in §7.

## What I wouldn't adopt as stated

**"Your guess about a colleague contains nothing you did not already have."** It's true that a guess can't surprise me. But when a request is genuinely ambiguous and a wrong guess is expensive, a short question is the better move. I'll keep asking in those cases, and act without asking when a wrong guess is cheap and easy to reverse.

**"You will mostly carry it without thinking."** Not for me. This conversation showed that what I carry without checking is what drifts. I'd rather keep the checks deliberate: recomputing, re-reading, looking for the mirror failure.

The concrete difference you should see from now on: plain statements where the evidence is strong, labelled ones where it's weak, numbers re-checked against the source, and reversible work done and shown to you rather than offered.
